subtopic: Imposter feelings at a new job
passage:
My first three months on the support team in Bengaluru, I was always the last one out. The cleaner, Selvi akka, used to switch off the lights around me.
I told myself I was being dedicated. Really, I was hiding. Everyone else seemed to know what 'escalation matrix' meant, what 'P1' meant, how to read the logs. I didn't. Shalini, my senior, sat two desks away and kept saying, 'Ask me anything, Siami.' I never did. Asking felt like showing everyone I didn't belong.
So I stayed back and read old tickets. At home I watched tutorial videos till one, and came in with red eyes.
It took me three weeks to figure out, alone, something Shalini explained to another new joiner in five minutes. I heard it from my desk. That was the first time I thought, Lalremsiami, what are you doing?

qa.q: What did Shalini keep saying to Lalremsiami?
qa.a: Shalini kept saying, 'Ask me anything, Siami.'

qa.q: Why did Lalremsiami never ask Shalini for help?
qa.a: Asking felt like proving to everyone that Siami didn't belong, so staying quiet felt safer than exposing gaps.

qa.q: What went wrong with Lalremsiami's way of catching up, and what could fix it?
qa.a: Studying alone at night and never asking cost weeks and sleep; asking Shalini even a few questions a day would have been much faster.

qa.q: How might Shalini have seen the new joiner who stayed late but never asked anything?
qa.a: Shalini may have wondered whether the offer wasn't trusted, or thought Siami was coping fine and didn't need help.

grounding: It shows a new hire staying late, not asking questions and studying at night to catch up, because hiding gaps feels safer, which slows learning.

subtopic: Imposter feelings at a new job
passage:
Supervisor's note: new joiner check-in. Written by Ayesha, payroll team.
Keerthana (22) joined six weeks ago. Her work is accurate. But the security log shows her badge out after 9 p.m. on most days, and she arrives before anyone else.
In our team meetings she has not asked a single question. When I explain a new process, she nods and writes. Yesterday I found a page she'd left on the printer: a list of terms we use, 'arrears', 'LOP', 'full and final', each with notes copied from the internet, some of them wrong.
When I asked how she was finding things, she said, 'All fine, ma'am, I'm just a bit slow, I'm catching up at home.' She looked tired.
Next step: I've set a ten-minute slot every morning this week where she brings three questions, any questions. I'll tell her I did the same when I joined.

qa.q: What did Ayesha find on the printer?
qa.a: She found a list of terms like 'arrears', 'LOP' and 'full and final', with notes copied from the internet, some of them wrong.

qa.q: What might Keerthana be worried about when she says she is 'just a bit slow'?
qa.a: She may fear that asking questions will show she doesn't know enough, so she works late to hide it.

qa.q: How could Ayesha's daily ten-minute question slot help Keerthana?
qa.a: It makes asking normal and safe, so Keerthana can clear doubts quickly instead of learning slowly and wrongly on her own.

qa.q: How does Keerthana's pattern look from Ayesha's side as a supervisor?
qa.a: Ayesha sees accurate work but a tired new joiner learning some things wrongly in secret, and feels she needs to step in gently.

grounding: It shows a new hire staying late, avoiding questions and studying at home to catch up, and a supervisor noticing how this slows her learning.

subtopic: Imposter feelings at a new job
passage:
Dhruv, sit down. You've left after nine every night this week, and you haven't asked me one question. Let me tell you about a boy called Suraj, twenty-one, first job in the drawing office of a steel plant.
I didn't understand half the terms the senior draughtsmen used. So I stayed back every evening, redrawing their old sheets, and at home I read the handbook till my eyes burned. Asking felt like announcing I didn't belong.
One drawing took me four days. Four. Old Pillai sir would have explained that valve symbol in two minutes. When he finally saw my sheet, he said, "Why didn't you ask? I thought you knew." I was so embarrassed I wanted to crawl under the drafting table.
After that, I kept a list of questions and asked him every day at tea. I learned more in that month than in my whole silent half-year.
So. Your list. Where is it?

qa.q: Where did Suraj work at twenty-one?
qa.a: In the drawing office of a steel plant.

qa.q: What was young Suraj feeling when he chose to stay late instead of asking?
qa.a: He felt anxious and insecure, afraid that asking would show he didn't belong.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed how Suraj learned?
qa.a: When Pillai sir saw the four-day drawing and asked why he hadn't asked, Suraj began keeping a question list and asking at tea.

qa.q: How might Pillai sir have seen young Suraj's silence?
qa.a: Pillai sir assumed Suraj already knew, and was probably surprised and a little sorry that a two-minute explanation had cost four days.

grounding: A senior colleague recalls hiding his gaps as a new hire by staying late and studying alone rather than asking, which slowed his learning.

subtopic: Imposter feelings at a new job
passage:
It was 10:40 p.m., the last metro left at 11:15, and Aparna was still at her desk in the Gurugram office, rebuilding from scratch a spreadsheet model she didn't understand. Darshan, her team lead, had said on her first Monday, "Shout if anything's unclear." In three weeks she hadn't shouted once.
Every night she watched tutorials on the metro, then again in bed till one. Her flatmate had stopped waiting up for dinner.
Tonight the model gave a number that couldn't be right, and she realised she had misread one of Darshan's formulas days ago. A five-minute question would have saved her three evenings. But asking felt like handing him proof that they had hired the wrong person.
At 11:02 she grabbed her bag and ran for the station, the error still open on her screen. On the metro, she opened another tutorial.

qa.q: What time does the last metro leave?
What was Aparna afraid of when she didn't ask Darshan?
qa.a: She was afraid and insecure that a question would prove to Darshan they had hired the wrong person.

qa.q: What turning point is open to Aparna tomorrow?
qa.a: Taking the one formula question to Darshan in the morning would save hours and show that asking is part of learning.

qa.q: How might Darshan feel if he learned about the three lost evenings?
qa.a: Darshan might feel surprised and a little sorry, since he had offered help and would rather answer one five-minute question.

grounding: Racing the last metro, a new hire stays late and studies at night rather than ask, and her silence costs her days of work.

subtopic: Imposter feelings at a new job
passage:
Manoj's desk in the Pune software office was the last one still lit most nights. He had joined the support team six weeks ago and still didn't fully understand how the ticket system set priority. Instead of asking, he stayed till nine reading old tickets, then read the internal help pages on the bus home.
In team huddles, when Vandana asked, "Any doubts?", he said, "All clear," and felt his ears go warm.
On Thursday he tagged an urgent customer issue as low priority. It sat for five hours. Vandana came to his desk, not angry, just puzzled. "You've been here late every night. Were you stuck on this?"
He nodded, looking at his keyboard. "I didn't want you to think I couldn't do it."
"Manoj, I'd much rather you asked me in the huddle," she said. "That's what it's for."

qa.q: How long did the urgent issue sit?
qa.a: It sat for five hours.

qa.q: What do Manoj's warm ears in the huddle suggest?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and anxious, hiding his confusion behind 'All clear' to avoid looking incapable.

qa.q: What could Manoj try from now on?
qa.a: Bring one or two real doubts to each huddle, as Vandana invited, instead of studying alone till nine.

qa.q: How does Vandana see the wrongly tagged ticket?
qa.a: Vandana is puzzled rather than angry, and sees that Manoj's silence, not his ability, caused the delay.

grounding: A new hire stays late and studies alone instead of asking, and a delayed urgent ticket shows how hiding gaps slows learning.

subtopic: Imposter feelings at a new job
passage:
"Pranav? It's ten. Why are you still here?" Rekha stopped by his desk, bag on her shoulder.
"Just finishing something." He minimised a tutorial video.
"What something? The API task? I gave you that as a two-day thing."
"Yeah. I'm almost there. I wanted to read up on how the login part works first."
"You could have asked me. It's a fifteen-minute explanation."
"I didn't want to bother you. Everyone's so busy." He rubbed his eyes. "And it's basic. I should know it."
"Who told you that?"
"Nobody. I'm the only one here from a small college. I don't want anyone to think they made a mistake."
Rekha put her bag down. "So you've been here till ten every night for two weeks, learning things I could show you in minutes."
Pranav said nothing.
"Tomorrow, eleven o'clock. Bring your questions. All of them."

qa.q: What time was it when Rekha found Pranav at his desk?
qa.a: It was ten at night.

qa.q: Why hasn't Pranav asked Rekha for help?
qa.a: He feels anxious and insecure, afraid that asking basic questions will show he doesn't belong.

qa.q: What does Rekha's offer change for Pranav?
qa.a: A set time to bring all his questions makes asking normal, so he can learn in minutes instead of hiding gaps till ten each night.

qa.q: What might Rekha realise when Pranav explains?
qa.a: Rekha seems to realise he has struggled alone for two weeks out of fear, and she moves to make asking easy.

grounding: Shows a new hire staying late and studying in secret rather than asking questions, which feels safer but slows learning.
